transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: Police in Singapore have reported a significant drop in shoplifting incidents at shopping malls across the city-state since they began using artificial intelligence-powered surveillance cameras earlier this year. The AI system uses computer vision technology to detect suspicious behavior, such as someone concealing items in their bags or clothing, and alerts security personnel in real time. In the first six months of operation, shoplifting arrests decreased by 45 percent compared to the same period last year. Retailers say they are also saving money on losses from stolen merchandise, which had been costing the industry millions of dollars annually. However, the technology has raised privacy concerns among some citizens, who worry about constant surveillance in public spaces. Authorities have responded that the cameras are only used in retail areas where there is already a reasonable expectation of security monitoring, and that footage is deleted after 30 days unless it is needed for an investigation. Several other countries are reportedly studying Singapore's system as a possible model for reducing retail crime.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: New research published in the Journal of the American Medical Association suggests that getting less than six hours of sleep per night on a regular basis can significantly increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease. The study, which followed over 4,000 healthy adults for a period of 10 years, found that participants who consistently slept fewer than six hours were 27 percent more likely to develop heart disease or suffer a stroke compared to those who slept seven to eight hours nightly. The researchers also found that poor sleep quality was associated with higher blood pressure, increased inflammation, and problems with blood sugar regulation—all risk factors for cardiovascular issues. What makes this study particularly significant is that it accounted for other factors that could affect heart health, such as smoking, exercise habits, and diet, and still found a strong correlation between insufficient sleep and cardiovascular risk. The study's lead author recommends that adults prioritize getting seven to eight hours of quality sleep each night, along with maintaining a healthy diet and regular exercise routine. Doctors say that establishing a consistent sleep schedule, avoiding screens before bedtime, and creating a dark, quiet sleep environment can all help improve sleep quality.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: A team of archaeologists working in Egypt has announced the discovery of a 3,000-year-old city that had been lost to the desert sands near Luxor. The ancient city, which dates back to the reign of King Amenhotep III, is one of the largest and best-preserved ancient Egyptian settlements ever found. Archaeologists began excavating the site last September, expecting to find a mortuary temple, but instead uncovered the remains of a complete city with houses, bakeries, workshops, and administrative buildings. Many artifacts have been found in excellent condition, including jewelry, pottery, tools, and even human remains. The site also contains evidence of daily life from the period, including cooking utensils, textile fragments, and children's toys. Egypt's former antiquities minister called the discovery the most important since the finding of Tutankhamun's tomb nearly a century ago, as it promises to shed new light on what life was like during one of Egypt's most prosperous periods. Excavation work is continuing at the site, and archaeologists say they expect to make many more discoveries in the coming months, including what they believe may be undiscovered tombs nearby.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Harper): Hey, Jackson. You look really stressed. Are you okay?
Man (Jackson): Not really, Harper. I'm trying to plan my schedule for next semester, and I just found out that two of the classes I need are offered at exactly the same time. I don't know what to do.
Woman: Oh, that's the worst! Which classes are conflicting?

Man: It's Advanced Statistics and Research Methods. Both are required for my psychology major, and they're both only offered next semester—if I don't take them now, I'll have to wait an entire year, which will delay my graduation.
Woman: Hmm, is there any chance they offer one of them online? Or maybe a night section?

Man: I checked already. No online sections for either, and both are only offered during the day on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I already emailed both professors to see if there's any possibility of attending one and watching recordings of the other, but neither of them records their lectures.

Woman: What about taking one of them at the community college over the summer? I know some people who've done that to get required classes out of the way. The credits usually transfer, and classes are smaller too.
Man: I thought about that, but I already have plans for the summer—I was supposed to do an internship that's really important for getting into grad school. I can't really back out of that now.

Woman: Wait, have you talked to your academic advisor? They might know about other options, or maybe they can help you get permission to substitute a different class. I remember when my roommate had a similar problem, her advisor found a special topics class that counted for one of the requirements.

Man: You're right, I should probably go see my advisor. I just haven't had time yet with midterms this week. Do you know where the advising office is? I've only been there once during freshman orientation.

Woman: It's in the Social Sciences building, room 203. They have walk-in hours on Wednesday afternoons, or you can make an appointment online through the student portal. If I were you, I'd try to make an appointment as soon as possible, though—they get really busy around registration time.
Man: I'll do that today, actually. Thanks for the suggestion, Harper. I was so focused on the problem that I didn't even think about talking to my advisor.
Woman: No problem at all! That's what advisors are there for. Let me know how it goes—I hope you can figure something out.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The concept of emotional intelligence, often referred to as EQ, has become increasingly popular in recent years, both in the workplace and in personal development. But what exactly is emotional intelligence, and why does it matter?

Emotional intelligence refers to the ability to recognize, understand, manage, and appropriately express our own emotions, as well as the ability to recognize, understand, and respond effectively to the emotions of others. Psychologists Peter Salovey and John Mayer first introduced the term in the early 1990s, and it was later popularized by journalist and psychologist Daniel Goleman in his 1995 book on the subject. Goleman identified five key components of emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills.

Self-awareness means being able to recognize and understand your own moods, emotions, and drives, as well as their effects on other people. Self-regulation involves being able to control or redirect disruptive impulses and moods, and thinking before acting. Motivation refers to a passion for working for reasons beyond money or status, and pursuing goals with energy and persistence. Empathy is the ability to understand the emotional makeup of other people and treat them according to their emotional reactions. Finally, social skills involve proficiency in managing relationships and building networks, and finding common ground with others.

Research has shown that emotional intelligence can be just as important as intellectual intelligence, or IQ, in determining success in many areas of life. In the workplace, studies have found that employees with higher EQ tend to be better at working in teams, handling stress, resolving conflicts, and providing leadership. This is why many companies now include emotional intelligence assessments as part of their hiring and promotion processes. In our personal lives, higher emotional intelligence is associated with better relationships, more effective communication, and greater overall well-being.

The good news is that unlike IQ, which remains relatively stable throughout life, emotional intelligence can be developed and improved with practice. Some ways to improve your EQ include paying attention to your own emotions and how they affect your behavior, practicing active listening when talking to others, trying to see situations from other people's perspectives, and taking responsibility for your actions when you make mistakes.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: The British seaside holiday has a long and fascinating history that reflects major social and economic changes in British society over the past 200 years. Before the 19th century, going to the seaside for pleasure was almost exclusively an activity for the wealthy upper classes. Seaside towns like Brighton and Scarborough developed as fashionable resorts where aristocrats would come to "take the waters" and socialize. Seawater was actually believed to have medicinal properties, and doctors would prescribe bathing in the sea as a treatment for various ailments.

The rise of the railways in the mid-19th century transformed seaside holidays entirely, making them accessible to working-class people for the first time. Railway companies began offering cheap day trips and holiday excursions to coastal towns, and workers in the new industrial cities could afford to take their families to the seaside for a day or even a week during the summer. Seaside towns grew rapidly to accommodate these new visitors, building piers, promenades, amusement arcades, and boarding houses. Traditional British seaside entertainment developed during this period, including Punch and Judy shows, donkey rides on the beach, fish and chip shops, and end-of-the-pier variety shows.

The post-World War II period saw the heyday of the British seaside holiday. With paid holiday leave becoming standard and increasing prosperity, millions of British families would take their annual summer holiday at a coastal resort. Butlins and other holiday camps became extremely popular, offering affordable all-inclusive holidays with accommodation, meals, and entertainment all on one site.

However, starting in the 1960s and 1970s, the traditional British seaside holiday began to decline as package holidays abroad became cheaper and more widely available. Mediterranean destinations like Spain, Greece, and Portugal offered guaranteed sunshine and warmer seas, and many British holidaymakers started traveling abroad instead. Many seaside towns fell into decline as visitor numbers dropped, with piers falling into disrepair and hotels closing.

In recent years, though, there has been something of a revival of the British seaside holiday. Rising costs of overseas travel, concerns about the environmental impact of flying, and a nostalgia for simpler holidays have led many people to rediscover the charms of British coastal towns. Many resorts have undergone major regeneration projects, and "staycations"—holidays spent at home or in one's own country—have become increasingly popular.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Have you ever wondered why you can remember events from your childhood with surprising clarity, but you can't remember what you had for lunch last Tuesday? Or why certain smells or songs can instantly bring back vivid memories from decades ago? Human memory is a complex and fascinating process that scientists are still working to fully understand.

Our memories are not stored like files on a computer, where each memory has its own specific location. Instead, memories are distributed across different regions of the brain and are reconstructed each time we recall them. This means that our memories are not perfect recordings of past events—they can change over time, and we can even develop false memories of things that never actually happened.

Memory is typically divided into three main stages: encoding, storage, and retrieval. Encoding is the process of getting information into our memory system in the first place. This happens automatically for some things—like an emotional event—but requires effort and attention for other information, like studying for an exam. Storage is maintaining information over time, and retrieval is the process of getting information back out when we need it.

There are also different types of memory. Short-term, or working memory, holds small amounts of information for brief periods, usually around 20 to 30 seconds, unless we actively rehearse it. Long-term memory, on the other hand, can store vast amounts of information for decades. Within long-term memory, there are further distinctions: explicit memories are facts and experiences we can consciously recall, like your best friend's birthday or what happened on your first day of school, while implicit memories are skills and procedures we don't have to consciously think about, like riding a bicycle or typing on a keyboard.

Several factors affect how well we remember things. Emotionally significant events tend to be remembered much better than neutral events, which is why many people have vivid "flashbulb memories" of where they were during major historical events. Repetition and rehearsal help strengthen memories, as does connecting new information to things we already know. Sleep also plays a crucial role in memory consolidation—the process by which short-term memories are converted into long-term storage.

Understanding how memory works can help us improve our ability to learn and remember information. Techniques like spacing out study sessions over time (rather than cramming), testing yourself on material, and making information meaningful by relating it to your own life can all significantly improve retention.
